'''Alfred Herbert Ltd''' was one of the world's largest [[machine tool]] manufacturing businesses. It was at one time the largest British [[machine tool builder]].<ref name="Floud2006-1976p43">{{Harvnb|Floud|2006|p=43}}.</ref>

==History==
The business was founded in 1888 when [[Alfred Herbert]] and [[William Hubbard (engineer)|William Hubbard]] purchased for £2,375 a small engineering business in Coventry.<ref name="odnb"/> ''Herbert & Hubbard'' initially made [[boiler]]s<ref name="LondonGazette18901216">{{London Gazette|issue=26115|page=7074|date=16 December 1890}}</ref> and [[steam engine]]s. The firm, in [[Roderick Floud]]'s paraphrasing of Herbert,<ref name="Floud2006-1976p43"/><ref name="Floud2006-1976p43_210">{{Harvnb|Floud|2006|pp=43, 210}}.</ref> "came into machine tool production by accident when Alfred Herbert secured the agency for a French patent of great value in the manufacture of tubes for the fast expanding cycle trade in Coventry. On the basis of his profits from this patent the company began to make machine tools for the cycle trade."

In 1894 Hubbard was bought out and the business continued as ''Alfred Herbert Ltd'' focusing on [[machine tool]]s.<ref name="LondonGazette18901216"/> The number of employees rose from 180 in 1897 to 1,400 by 1908.<ref>DR. A. SHADWELL, ''Special Articles. Selected British Industries'', [[The Times]], 4 March 1908</ref>
[[File:Herbert Art Gallery and Museum, Coventry - Lathe.jpg|thumb|left|A Herbert Lathe on display in [[Herbert Art Gallery and Museum]].]]
Regarding the differences (real or supposed) between American and British practice in the latter half of the 19th century, Floud<ref name="Floud2006-1976p56">{{Harvnb|Floud|2006|p=56}}.</ref> said that Herbert was "the [British] firm often held up as an example of the use of American techniques" [which sometimes emphasised focus on a narrow range of machines by any one builder] but that even Herbert "rejected the idea that the firm should specialize in a few types of machinery" [to the exclusion of a diverse mix of products]. He quoted Herbert as saying that "the cycle business, which was our principal customer, required in those days a variety of machines, and not many of them of one kind."<ref name="Floud2006-1976p56"/>

The firm was known for technical excellence<ref name="Floud2006-1976p34">{{Harvnb|Floud|2006|p=34}}.</ref> and competed well against other brands, especially in [[turret lathe]]s.<ref name="Floud2006-1976p74">{{Harvnb|Floud|2006|p=74}}, citing Carden 1909–1910, p. 225.</ref> The foreign-sales efforts of the Herbert firm are touched on in Floud's discussion of machine tool exports.<ref name="Floud2006-1976p87-89">{{Harvnb|Floud|2006|pp=87–89}}.</ref>

In 1899 a foundry was built at [[Edgwick]] where most of the Company's operations were subsequently based.<ref name="odnb">[http://www.oxforddnb.com/view/article/48619?docPos=2 Alfred Herbert at Oxford Dictionary of National Biography]</ref> During the first half of the twentieth century it became one of the largest [[machine tool]] manufacturers in the world.<ref name="Lloyd-Jones_and_Lewis_2006_p4">{{Harvnb|Lloyd-Jones|Lewis|2006|p=4}}.</ref>

By the 1930s '''Alfred Herbert Limited''' was making profits around £600,000 (''2011: £{{formatnum:{{Inflation|UK|586149|1939|2011|r=-4}}}}'') . The company was listed on the [[London Stock Exchange]] in March 1944 and the following year described its business as "Machine Tool Makers, Importers and Factors, and [[Mechanical Engineers]] etc". The main works covered 22 acres in [[Coventry]] and the company had operations in [[Argentina]], France, [[India]], Australia and "in normal times", Italy.<ref>Display Advertising: ''Alfred Herbert Limited'' ''[[The Times]]'', 30 October 1945</ref> It acquired ''Sigma Instruments'' in 1948.<ref name="odnb"/>

In 1975, following sustained losses, the company asked the [[National Enterprise Board]] to invest £25 million in the business to provide for modernisation and to reduce borrowings.<ref name="Lloyd-Jones_and_Lewis_2006_p316">{{Harvnb|Lloyd-Jones|Lewis|2006|p=316}}.</ref> The Company was then renamed ''Herbert Ltd''.<ref name="Lloyd-Jones_and_Lewis_2006_p316"/> In the late 1970s there was an escalation of machine tool imports into the United Kingdom that left the Company behind.<ref name="Lloyd-Jones_and_Lewis_2006_p317">{{Harvnb|Lloyd-Jones|Lewis|2006|p=317}}.</ref>

The business was acquired by ''Tooling Investments'' in 1980 but then went into [[receivership]] in 1982.<ref name="Lloyd-Jones_and_Lewis_2006_p317"/> The assets were bought by [[TI Group|Tube Investments]] later that year, but the business closed in 1983.<ref>[https://api.parliament.uk/historic-hansard/commons/1983/jul/25/west-midlands Paragraph 879, House of Commons Debates] Hansard, 25 July 1983.</ref>
